newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Iron ore lures investors in CVRD sell-off.
newsitem.headline: Iron ore lures investors in CVRD sell-off.

text.p: Thirty years ago, a geologist in search of manganese landed his helicopter in a remote region of Brazil's Amazon for refueling only to stumble across 18 billion tons of iron ore -- the largest deposit in the world.

Today the Carajas mining district in Brazil's northern Para state is the hottest asset on the books of state mining giant Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (CVRD) and the prize everyone is after in the company's forthcoming privatisation.

Not only does it hold enough iron ore to secure 400 years of production, but it is rich in other minerals as well, especially gold. It is speculated that hundreds of tons of gold are waiting to be unearthed in the Carajas region.

"What everyone is after is the iron ore," said independent mining consultant Peter Rich. "There is only one attraction: Carajas. It is the biggest iron ore deposit in the world and it is very well run."

CVRD invested $3 billion to develop Carajas into what it is today, a mining fiefdom complete with a company town, a railway to transport the iron ore to the coast and a deep water port in Maranhao state.

International mining companies, steelmakers and iron ore traders are scrambling to join forces and snatch up a strategic 45 percent block of CVRD voting shares when it goes on sale April 29 for a base price of 3 billion reais ($2.83 billion).

This will be followed by a staff and global offer later in the year to sell off the government's entire 51 percent stake in the world's largest iron ore producer and exporter, valued at a total of 10.36 billion reais ($9.77 billion).
The Japanese want it to secure the supply of natural resources for their huge steel industry, while the Brazilians want it to keep the country's mineral wealth in domestic hands.
The Australians want it to boost their influence in the iron ore market and the South Africans want it to diversify their mining operations outside South Africa.

But some big market players have found the privatisation rules discouraging because they limit large iron ore producers, buyers and traders to a 10 percent stake in any consortium bidding in the sell-off.
This complicates the formation of consortia, each of which has to include at least three companies, and decreases the chances of having many bidders at the auction.

"When the government imposed these restrictions, it took the risk of alienating many big players," said Julio Carvalho, the financial director in Brazil for the Anglo-Australian mining group RTZ-CRA. "Three (consortia) is unlikely. There will be one or two."
The government hopes there will be at least two consortia competing for the 45 percent block, ensuring that the auction achieves a premium on the minimum price.
Three consortia are taking shape so far, one of which is fairly advanced while the other two are still tenuous.
Brazilian metal, cement and pulp group Votorantim has teamed up with South Africa's Anglo American Corp. of South Africa Ltd. and Banco Safra and is in talks with Japan's Nippon Steel Corp.
It is the most established consortium and tipped to be the government's favourite because of its nationalist credentials.

Brazil's largest steelmaker Companhia Siderurgica Nacional (CSN) is also determined to launch a bid, but is finding it more difficult forming a group of investors after two potential partners, retail bank Banco Bradesco SA and South Africa's Gencor Ltd., dropped out of the race.
The third consortium could consist of Brazilian metals and mining group Caemi Mineracao e Metalurgia SA, Japan's Mitsui & Co. Ltd. and Australian mining firm WMC Ltd.

CVRD is Latin America's largest privatisation to date and expected to net the government at least $5 billion, that is $2 billion more than the region's previous record privatisation of Argentine oil firm YPF.

It is seen internationally as proof of the Brazil's resolve to open its economy and embrace liberal economic principles. It also boosts the credibility of Brazil's privatisation programme, often criticised for being slow.

Critics say the government is selling off the country's mineral wealth for a pittance and undermining national sovereignty, but President Fernando Henrique Cardoso has shrugged off those comments as backward and uninformed.

"There are many people who don't understand modern processes and don't understand that a well-conceived privatisation of a company that the government does not benefit from owning protects our assets," Cardoso said.

Planning Minister Antonio Kandir calculated that the government's $5 billion stake in CVRD costs the Brazilian people at least $430 million a year in funds which could be spent on important social programmes.
He said the government only received $70 million in annual dividends from CVRD, but if the $5 billion were invested elsewhere the return would be at least $500 million per year.
